Allan. Finally, this book was made for the Stonypathians, Ian, Sue and Ailie. x i x I was born, quite inappropriately, in Nassau, Bahamas. My father was engaged in bootlegging at the time. My parents are both Scottish and my father’s father was head forester on a Scottish estate. While still small I was sent home to boarding school in Scotland, but then my father, having lost all his money orange farming in Florida, returned to Scotland, and I went to live with my parents in Glasgow. When the war began in 1939 I was evacuated to the country, and this was the end of my formal education; I spent most of my time fishing in wee burns. In due course I was conscripted and spent four years in the army. After the war I got married and worked as a shepherd; but I had a dream of young men engaged in learned discourse while strolling on lawns. This led me to give up being a shepherd and try to live off trout and stewed rabbits. I also read books on philosophy from the public library. It was then that I started to write. At first I wrote little ‘descriptions’ of ‘nature’, and then short stories, some of which were published. My very first published work was a little ‘nature essay’ (not the custom ary début of an avant garde writer) which I submitted to a newspaper under a pseudonym. It was rejected, but when I later sent it in acciden tally to the same paper under my own name, it was published at once. A u T O b iO g r A p h iC A l S k E T C h Note: This draft autobiographical statement was dictated by Ian Hamilton Finlay to his friend Lesley Lendrum. Previously unpublished, this transcription slightly revises the original handwritten manuscript. x x \ a u t o b i o g r a P h i c a l s k e t c h My stories began to have fewer descriptions and more & more dialogue, finally turning into plays. (Several of my one act plays were broadcast by the BBC.) A collection of my plays was published in German trans lation in Vienna a decade later. My great difficulty in writing stories & plays was to find how to put words together so that the result was

neither working nor middle class, but ‘human’, like Chekov. Then I knew scarcely any writers as friends. My chief friend was the local thief who gave me soup in his low ceilinged, smoke blackened kitchen. I also worked as a casual labourer now & then. It was at this time that I began to suffer from nervous anxiety. It was, and is, unpleasant, but no more interesting, really, than toothache. I went to the city for treatment; my marriage came to an end. As soon as I could, I went to Orkney, where I started to write poetry. Here I had the same problem—how to put words together—essentially a problem of syntax, the lack of which was to be such a feature of concrete poetry. My poems were eventually published by the Migrant Press, Ventura, California. Through this I got to know other poets by letter: Jonathan Williams, Robert Creeley. I returned to the city & started the Wild Hawthorn Press, consequently having to encounter the Scottish hostil ity to the idea of lyric poetry, foreign poetry & ‘modern’ literature. I am now settled (touch wood) on the Scottish mainland. I live in the country & work at concrete poetry. It is impossible to describe con crete poetry in a few sentences, but I feel it is relevant because it is concerned with intelligence & order, not the self, ‘thought’ & fuss. I am not interested in ‘experiment’ but in avant garde work which can take the creative step backwards to join with the past. I consider ‘experi ment’ in all fields old fashioned; where so much that was ‘given’ is now man made, the aim should be choice—i.e. the measure of science & the arts should be decency, not the self dramatisation of man. I have become interested also in concrete poetry in relation to archi a u t o b i o g r a P h i c a l s k e t c h / x x i tecture & avant gardening. This is not a whim, but the logical develop ment of earlier concrete poetry—from the poem as an object on the page to the poem as an object properly realised in sandblasted glass, stone or indeed concrete. The poem I see as the centre of order and calm & abiding values—the opposite of the idea of ‘confessional’ poetry. I also continue publishing, believing

in the lyrical, in intelligence, not in ‘thought’. I believe also that there is no need for Scotland to be different from other nations. We should have a contemporary literature like everywhere else. Ian Hamilton Finlay Gledfield, March 1966 CURFEW / curlew (1971). A one-word poem in the hillside garden at Stonypath. Ian Hamilton Finlay with Sue Finlay, lettercarving by Vincent Butler. Photograph by Robin Gillanders, 2002 (original photograph in colour). 1 Ian Hamilton Finlay, letters; Alec Finlay, stitches Standing on the edge of a heather moor where the Pentland Hills rise is a whinstone boulder with a single vein of quartz. This stone is a poem. Inscribed ‘CURFEW / curlew ’, it invites us to hear the bird’s liquid call as it plies its oracular flight down to the valley below. 1 The transition of letters—inward folded ‘ f ’ for alert ‘ l ’—translates natural song into human alarm. As the evening shadows gather we slip into exile; the toc sin tolls and it is time we were safely home from the hill. Imaginatively we have entered Stonypath, Little Sparta, genius loci of Ian Hamilton Finlay. Further on we may wander into ‘a small grove composed of young pine trees and delicate columns. All the needles which fall from the trees are carefully swept into heaps around the foot of the columns.’ 2 A poem in slate catches the branches’ outline and, as the breezes shush, we read another inscription: ‘WOOD / WIND / SONG, WIND / SONG / WOOD, WOOD / WIND / SONG’. The poem belongs here because this is where the poet first heard the wind. 3 Carved, the words suggest permanence; sun and shade, wind, birdsong, the transitory effects of nature, they too are integral to the garden poem. More than any other poet of the modern era, Finlay realized the potential of the poem as an object that belongs within an ‘environ ment’—though he would doubtlessly have preferred the term ‘gar den’, ‘grove’ or ‘landscape’. T o the adventurous he is an ‘ A V ANT i N Tr O d u C T iO N : p iC k iN g T h E l A S T w i l d F l O w E r 2 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n GARDEner’, pioneering poems in glass, aluminum and neon sited in

parks and landscapes throughout the world. T o the traditionalist his oeuvre is a belated recovery of Antique styles and age old skills, eulo gizing pastoral fishing boats and wildflowers. Recent critical accounts conjure the garden as cynosure for a reclusive Neoclassical ‘genius’, whereas, for the poet, its status was elusive—inevitably so, given it was Stonypath, his fond home, and Little Sparta, his martial state, complete with stamps, medals, monuments, a flag and Garden T emple. 4 The poet’s remarkable letters reveal a lyric sensitivity and riven identity, for Finlay was a ‘makar’ whose expansive poetics arose from a homesickness that was life defining, his vision shadowed by a pro found sense of cosmological division: ‘The sum of my work is tragic. But it is centred on the lyrical; so much of it is pastoral, Virgilian.’ 5 If readers wish, they can enter this poetic domain, even touch the text with their fingertips. Finlay belonged to that generation of innova tors who grasped the means of poetic production. Embracing the text as a Platonic essence which must then be embodied—not in a voice projected, but as a thing placed, rooted even. Each poem carried the potential to assume different guises, through the careful choice of type face, printed format or material; each word weighted or floated within its own space. For outdoor poems he devised composed landscapes. For indoor poems there were the myriad forms of typeface, card, print and book. These diverse settings are largely absent in this volume: the decision to adopt a uniform design style for Selections is supported by Finlay’s own preference for standardized collections, such as Honey by the Water (1972) and The Blue Sail (2002). There was a constant interplay in Finlay’s imagination, between generic landscapes imbued with a painterly vision and magical encoun ters, such as those with the curlew, or the skylarks whose songs gave measure to family walks around the moor . I can still hear my father looking out the window, saying, ‘Sue—come and look at the light’. He i n t r o d u c t i o n / 3 briefly trained as an artist; after laying down his brushes, he remained a painter in outlook. 6 His celebrated garden—born of a youthful dream of philosophers wandering a classical landscape—composed views which he ‘signed’ after his beloved painters, Claude, Poussin, Friedrich and Corot. His subtle response to

place depended upon his painterly imagination; but, invited to create works of art for distant landscapes, he also depended on a particular gift for collaboration. Illness prevented him leaving home, and the work of scoping and installing was carried out by his wife, Sue, and latterly, by Pia Maria Simig. His poem objects were created with gifted collaborators. He also collaborated intellectu ally with critics, most notably an ongoing dialogue with his preferred commentator, Stephen Bann. 7 Finlay began as an author of short stories and plays, yet he came to reject ‘secular’ prose, setting aside consecutive sentences in favour of the aphorism—which he likened to the philosopher’s ‘hand grenade’. 8 The inclusion here of a generous selection of his detached sentences allows the reader to enjoy the poems alongside their witty companions. His later poems were themselves frequently imaginative collaborations with the past, employing found text, bibliography and interpolation. These collaborative impulses and strategies were expansive. They arise from the poet’s contested relation to authority, a theme that can be traced back to the early Kafkaesque fable, ‘The Money’ (1954), where the artist moved with an absolute sense of truth, resigns from society— a breach that would vigorously reassert itself in later disputes. The character of the artist in this story is a grown up version of the children who appear in other stories and plays of the era: the wee boys who roam secret glens; the teenage girls walking the tide line ‘like dancers—like on a tightrope’; each set apart from the world of adult authority. Later he would sacrifice such symbolic characters: ‘I wanted to revive an old tradition, of poets, philosophers, artists, craftsmen, work ing together, towards a common aim, with good will [. . .] I set out to 4 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n make works which bore no trace of the personality of Ian Hamilton Finlay (though that, of course, as I also know, is what has made them immediately identifiable as Finlay’s, in another way)’. 9 Sharing the authority of poesis, he believed that the gap between two people was a generative space into which the muses slipped. Declaring his garden retreat ‘an attack’, the ‘Jacobin’ Finlay confronted contemporary cul ture with the higher authority of the classical tradition. 10 Inscribing a domain in which the poet philosopher could once again hold sway, his

fictional children grew into the young revolutionary Saint Just, inter rogating liberal democracy with taboo imagery of power. These principles were actualized in a series of disputes or ‘wars’, as Finlay reacted fiercely to hostile critical judgments or threats to his garden republic. 11 Fury urged him on, and, in a paean to creativity, he confessed that, for him, art sprang from a thunderous intensity of feel ing: ‘what I get in certain moments is a really wild excitement about my work and a feeling of “fantastic”, if some great clash of ideologies is occurring, or when I conceive of a new kind of work. It’s those kind of moments on a tightrope that are extraordinary. I don’t know, it’s like being on the peak of two searchlights that have crossed and the feeling it’s not really you but you’re carrying this thing along.’ 12 The glare of these twin beams would in time draw him to eras of historical tragedy, the Third Reich and the French Revolution, which he replayed as myth and allegory. The vertiginous shifts of form and subject matter—early plays, stories and poems, lyrical portraits of the Scottish Highlands; non didactic Concrete poems of the 1960s; garden poetry of the 1970s; didactic revolutionary poems from his armed domain in the 1980s; the late return to the pastoral of the 1990s—can only be grasped in terms of the drama of the poet’s life. For all his rejection of psychologism and disapproval of biography, Finlay self dramatised his anomie to an extraordinary degree. Conflict is inherent to his psyche: it cannot i n t r o d u c t i o n / 5 be reconciled, must not be pacified. Some critics have concealed his intimate life and glossed over his engagement with power, estranging the work from tensions the poet insisted upon. 13 His quarrels began as variants on that longstanding Scottish literary tradition, the ‘flyt ing’, but he chose to translate his later disputes—some sought, others imposed—into the ‘clash of ideologies’, ‘wars’, exposing tensions he was determined our age should confront. 14 Finlay was the greatest Scottish writer of letters since Robert Louis Stevenson; letters were his favourite emblem of friendship, his primary method of working with collaborators, and his weapon of choice. Extracts from his vital, warm, sometimes stormy correspondence are stitched together here so the reader can follow his ideas as they evolve,

and compare them with the thoughtful residue of his sentences. Finlay’s maxims amuse and provoke. His ‘Table Talk’ has vim and tang, and his passionate belief in the spiritual role of culture and the non commercial potential of art continue to resonate. Some attitudes will be judged contrarian: however we negotiate his politics, much is forgiven by the charm of Domestic Pensées (2004) and the touching ‘Detached Sentences on Exile’ (1983), which so clearly reveal the ori gins of his rage in feelings of homesickness. Finally the reader has the necessary material to hand with which to illuminate the ‘tightrope’ Finlay trod, between animus and sensitivity; traumatized relation to the social world and commitment to friendship; fragility before wild nature and devotion to the garden. In his later years he liked to say that he was not a poet at all, but a ‘revolutionary’. Selections reinstates the truly radical nature of Finlay’s project, for his output is a diverse and generous index of poetic potential, and this remains his most revolu tionary achievement. 15 Finlay’s enactment of a poetics stilled in stone, subject to the flux of nature, was intimately connected in his imagination with the har mony of oppositions, as an early letter to Ernst Jandl makes clear: ‘I 6 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n have never sorted a garden before and it is very fascinating—it certainly gives one a very clear idea of impermanency, and of the power of time, grass, and weeds, the fragility, and beauty, of order.’ 16 His commitment to the landscape garden tradition would coincide with his discovery of Heraclitus—a philosopher whom Finlay acclaimed as the father of the thunderbolt, warring elements and form, as if to show his distaste for flux. 17 Despite the Enlightenment tenor of the gardener poet’s dis course with history and philosophy, his engagement with language remained divinatory. From the moment he settled at Stonypath, the act of naming rediscovered its fundamental importance. It is the principle which illuminates his one word poems, found poems, adapted alpha bets, poetic fragments, anagrams as well as the minimal operations enacted in IDYLLS (1987). Naming is by turns division, divination and revelation; the poet a harbinger, revealing concealed meanings, hidden relationships, bound oppositions. We may struggle to follow the Heraclitean Finlay over the years that followed, as the Virgilian lemon shaped fishing boat gives

way to the sublime mountain ravine guillotine, but the rhyme of mean ing resounds implacably. The great adventure of the garden refined these generative procedures in a way no other contemporary poet had achieved: it remains the decisive chiasma in his poetics, leading even tually—and in his mind, inevitably—to his dedication of the entire domain to the poetic muses, as ‘Little Sparta’. c h i l d h o o d , y o u t h Ian Hamilton Finlay was born in the Bahamas in 1925; he and his sister Ann were brought up on the island by Jim Finlay and his wife, Annie. His earliest memory, and one he would return to time after time in his later work, was the aptly romantic image of his boyhood self on a boat, his father’s schooner, which was hired out for pearl i n t r o d u c t i o n / 7 fishing and, much to Annie’s disapproval, running bootleg rum to Prohibition America. The small family fortune was lost when their Floridian orange plantation was ruined by successive bad winters. Aged only six, Ian was sent back to Scotland to board at Larchfield Academy, Helensburgh, where he saw his first warships sailing down the Clyde, and where he was taught by W . H. Auden. In the holidays he sometimes visited the grand home of a classmate, Charles Rennie Mackintosh’s masterpiece, Hill House. 18 His formal education con tinued at Dollar Academy, under the splendour of Playfair’s Doric façade. Exiled from his island home, the unhappy schoolboy made a den among the shrubbery defended by a brick and string booby trap, and when, inevitably, an unfortunate boy had his head broken , the hideaway was thrashed . He also endured the Dickensian Christmas ritual of the class fight over a bowl of crusts. When the Floridian plantation failed he had to leave Dollar. His poem ‘End of a Holiday’ is a wistful portrait of the reunited family holidaying on the Isle of Arran. 19 Another memory was of the splendour of Hopetoun House on the outskirts of Edinburgh, where his grandfather was in charge of the estate sawmill and his uncle night watchman, and where, unusu ally, he was allowed to play in the ‘big house’. The outbreak of war disrupted his schooling. He writes Ernst Jandl: ‘This is the anniversary of the start of

the war (for Britain). Third September ’39 I was a wee boy with a label round his neck, newly evacuated (from the city) to a little Highland village. No school, but pinewoods, wee burns, rabbits, trout, salmon, mountains . . . w hat happiness’. 20 This village, Gartmore, was where he built his first boat, a wooden canoe. Another idyll is recorded in his late prose poem ‘Cinema Going’ (1998), describing a cosy night out with his Aunt ‘T ot’ (Arabella Pettigrew) in St Andrews. Back in Glasgow, he disliked his new city school and left at fourteen. He never forgot the terror of the Clydebank Blitz (13–14 March 1941), which he endured shelter 8 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n ing with his family under a kitchen table. Thereafter, whenever there was a thunderstorm, he would go to bed and pull the covers tight over his head. T o Derek Stanford he portrays the ‘blitz’ of an apocalyp tic Perthshire thunderstorm: ‘ Are you afraid of thunder? I am terri fied. We were shaken about like crumbs inside a paper bag which was blown up with boiling air and then abruptly burst. The house rocked to and fro, and terrible lightnings crackled towards the climax. It was like waiting for the last of a stick of bombs.’ 21 The poet made light of this trauma in the pensée, ‘Idylls end in thunderstorms.’ 22 However, the lightning flash remained associated with the terrifying hail of bombs, and the bruise of war would eventually rise to the surface as an arsenal of warships and planes, symbolic of the Heraclitean fire. What then of the reality of conflict? Finlay joined the Non Combatant Corps in the latter part of the Second World War, seeing no active service. 23 He recalls rattling through Holland on a troop train, an image translated into the early Concrete poem the horizon of Holland is all ears (1965). 24 While stationed at Paderborn he was struck by the juxtaposition of rows of German tanks massed alongside an intact Neoclassical building—a subject he would return to in The Third Reich Revisited (1982). Finlay was an autodidact. He entered Glasgow School of Art at six teen, but was suspended in his first year as a punishment for organis ing a student strike. For a while he worked as the school’s janitor. He

never doubted that he would be an artist and while still in his youth, encountered the likes of John Middleton Murray, Dylan Thomas, and painters such as J. D Fergusson and ‘the two Roberts’ (Colquhoun and MacBryde), Joan Eardley, and his future collaborator Margot Sandeman. Derek Stanford recalls ‘a fair haired and faunlike creature,’ who would light up of a sudden, his face twitching ‘into wild vivacity and mirth.’ 25 On his return from Germany, Finlay settled in Glasgow, marry i n t r o d u c t i o n / 9 ing the artist Marion Fletcher (1922–1981). At their wedding his best man was the leading Scottish poet of the day, Hugh MacDiarmid (Christopher Murray Grieve). Then, abandoning the city, he wrote to Stanford, ‘I’m finished with the racket, meaning the town, friends, poetry, patter, etc.—that includes politics too—it’s all past hope— past despair too which is a profound comment. I reject the whole situation and am determined to make my life outside it.’ 26 Marion found a home for them in the Highlands, first at Invergeldie Farm, Glen Lednock, and then over the hill at Druim na Cille, a cottage gifted to them by her father, on the Dunira Estate. 27 T o his friend J. F. Hendry he described, ‘a whole world in Perthshire that is as unique as Faulkner’s Deep South—no one is aware of it. No writers I mean.’ 28 At Invergeldie The Soup (early 1950s). Portrait of Ian Hamilton Finlay and his wife Marion in their Perthshire cottage, by their friend Bet Low (1924–2007). Courtesy of Perth Museum and Art Gallery. 1 0 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n he worked as a shepherd with his dog Finn MacCool. Fifty years later he memorialised this period of his life in a traditional ‘drystane’ wall bearing a quotation in Gaelic: ‘SE TOISEACH IS DEIREADH AN DUINE A ’ BHUACHAILLEACHD’ (THE BEGINNING AND END OF LIFE IS HERDING). 29 This landscape of ‘bleak stone’ and ‘leaning firs’ is the world of his early short stories, poems and plays, such as ‘The Estate Hunters’, with its heartfelt idyll of a cottage with a lamp burning: ‘ And of course there’ll be a burn, too. And it’ll never have been fished. Not once. And so the trout—they’ll be so inno cent . . . A ll night they’ll be

rising like mad, and –. Oh, Daddy, Daddy, it will be so wonderful! We’ll never—neither of us—sleep a wink all night—not a wink all night—for the rises—of the trout!! (The stage turns to darkness. The window throws its golden light on their faces. They are smiling and crying.) ’ 30 Druim na Cille was ‘an extraordinary landscape of pines and mountains which I still owe many poems to’, and ‘bittersweet, like a mixture of Heine and Trakl.’ 31 The whitewashed cottage bears an uncanny resemblance to Stonypath: at the edge of habitation reached by stony tracks, facing southwest over a conspectus—the ‘Stonypathian vale’, and its counterpart the sacred hill of Saint Fillan. In these glens he had a dream of ‘young men engaged in learned discourse’, a vision that would eventually become the garden where the thought of Hegel, Schelling and Heidegger was actualised as herm, stile and wood path. 32 The fallen columns in the ruined formal garden at Dunira foretold those the poet would lodge among Stonypath’s moorland grasses; just as the Boltachan burn inspired the garden rill that he constructed in the early 1990s, complete with planted ferns, feeding the ‘Upper Pool’. 33 The more one reflects on his biography the more clear it is that each new landscape of home became, in time, a created landscape, shaped by the memory of a lost idyll. At Dunira he began as a painter who wrote short stories and became i n t r o d u c t i o n / 1 1 a playwright who wrote poems. A return visit brings this touching anecdote: Seeing my wee cottage with Edinburgh eyes, I thought it very nice, a bit like Van Gogh’s at Arles. The village children had broken in, and got hold of my oil paint, and, across the wall where I’d hung my pictures, written: ‘You are a lovely artist.’ Then a lot of kisses in red and blue. I was rather touched. [ . . . ] I k new I could write OK if I went back; it is quite another world, with mountains, and people, and a life, a real life. Only it is the past. Even if the future is a blank, that is what one must live towards. 34 By the end of the 1950s he had abandoned this fond world and, as if to mark the decisiveness of this

ending, he destroyed all his paint ings. His letters describe landscapes painted in a bittersweet Northern style influenced by Emil Nolde and Oscar Kokoscha. 35 He worked up an unpublished early version of his stories, titled The Blue Suited Fisherman, illustrated with his own drawings, ‘presenting entire one atmosphere.’ 36 When they eventually appeared as The Sea Bed and Other Stories (1958), they were illustrated with mournful woodcuts by Zeljko Kujundzic. 37 Writing to Stanford, he explains that he seeks a prose that is ‘simple but carefully shorn’, and expressed his desire ‘to write black bread prose, now, not Rye Vita as you were kind enough to say of that in my dialogue. I find it difficult to write simply, and I am of the opinion that what is demanded is above all a moral effort.’ An intrinsic ‘Scotch’ sadness is redeemed by ‘trout, burns, boys, old men, rain, black tea, woodbines, bracken, campfires, tents, pipes, etc.’, subjects which would continue to offer comfort for years to come. 38 Already he insisted all forms of art must be wedded to morality, ‘the great sin is to isolate technique, which then becomes a commodity, bought and sold.’ And he held to a T olstoyan abhorrence of ‘art as a vested interest—as a commodity “sold” in art schools—if only all the painters could be persuaded to stop selling to dealers & so on! The art 1 2 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n racket must be broken . . . O Fat old dealers, O Art School Professors, O shoddy virtuosos—you all are going to hell.’ 39 Finlay spoke of his stories’ ‘deep intuitive affinities with the non Classical culture of the North’ (jacket blurb, Sea Bed, probably by IHF). From the Highland fishing stories of the 1950s to the Arcadian groves of the 1970s, there is a continuity in the way each landscape was refined by the imagination’s recuperative powers, deeply felt, or as he might say, ‘redeemed’. This was all the more necessary as his life changing illness, agoraphobia, imposed itself during his stay in Perthshire. He was hos pitalised in 1954, following his first breakdown, which coincided with the beginning of the failure of his marriage to Marion. 40 For a while he took refuge in Balquhidder, with his friend Crombie Saunders in what was once a dog kennel. It is small

and whitewashed; the dogs have nibbled the door and the rain has nibbled the ceiling. There is one very small window, high in the wall, and all together it’s like a monk’s cell. I like it very much. I don’t know how long I can stay here, and after wards I don’t know at all. It is quite near my own house, and it seems strange that I just can’t go there, where my books and my table, and all, await. I have been out a few steps, but my legs still, alas, get shaky, and the fear begins, the further I go from the house . . . so metimes I realise that I am at the world’s mercy because of being ill, and that to be settled is only a dream. 41 It would be many years before that dream found reality. From 1955 to 1965 Finlay flitted between city flats and provisional country cot tages, spells of hope dashed by poverty, illness, loneliness or quarrels. In the summer of 1956 he was unhappy to be back in Glasgow: ‘I don’t want to finish any writing when I am in a city, amid alien shapes. If only I could get well enough to arrange for a place, and to make an order. I loved my shed at Drum na Keil, its tarred, leaky roof, the wee windows full of mountains and pines, and the big table that was the table on which the shepherds ate at the gatherings in the years before.’ 42 i n t r o d u c t i o n / 1 3 T o Cid Corman, editor of Origin, he characterised his anxiety: ‘ At times I feel a kind of beauty, movement of, too much—it’s to the world as a robin to a pine, it can’t nest there. I get overwhelmed. Or perhaps it’s more like having no father—no Father there.’ 43 A letter to George Mackay Brown outlines an emblematic story, ‘Lost’ (now itself lost), about a wee boy or a soul which wishes only to be left alone. It (he) runs away from the house full of adults, into the middle of a moor, where he lies down. Suddenly a little girl appears, in a sun hat, carrying flowers she has picked. She drifts nearer to him like a slow sailboat—‘she trailed one hand over the stern of the

boat, and the bow was heaped with pretty flowers.’ He waits still, then leaps up on her, and the flowers are all scattered. He speaks, and she doesn’t answer, so at length he realises she’s deaf. Then he picks up the flowers, pulls their heads off, and uses them to spell a word for her. He writes, ‘LO’, but then he has no more flowers, and he has to stop and gather more. Then he suddenly gets bored, and writes instead, ‘ST’. She looks at the word, and thinks he’s really lost, so she takes him to the path, then sets off, leaving him. He wanders all about till after sunset, then goes home . . . I t is a very strange story. I would write it if I had my big table! 44 s P e c t a t o r , c i r c u s - M a s t e r , n a v i g a t o r In a rite familiar to Scottish writers, Finlay found refuge on an island, Rousay, one of Orkney’s smaller islands. 45 In 1955 Marion found them a house named Wychwood, in Brinian; later he lived alone in a block built cottage at Sourin, described in his poem ‘Finlay’s House (on Rousay)’. 46 His longing for the island never left and, in a letter sent from a psychiatric ward in hospital, in 1961, he complained: ‘This is one of the first spring days, with sunshine; it is reminding me miserably of Rousay and of how hopeful I was there at first; how, even, enthusiastic, excited, at the actual things around me—a state I can only remember now, and feel as something back in the past. Perhaps it could all return 1 4 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n if circumstances were changed. And yet, one could never feel about Christmas again in that way, so why does one assume that other feelings are immortal in one?’ 47 Plaintive memory always associated itself with the lost idylls of childhood. The bounded nature of islands assuaged his anxiety, in the same way that a poem was capable of defining ‘clarity and goodness’. 48 Similar sentiments recur in later proverbs: ‘Illness and exile restore our horizons to us’, and, ‘When our friends leave us they take away our shores’. 49

At the time, Rousay seemed to represent ‘a last attempt to have a home.’ 50 Even safely settled at Stonypath he was still lamenting to Emmett Williams, ‘I will never see Orkney again—what an awful word is “never.” ’51 But the poet did, for one of his last land scape projects was a monumental inscription from Virgil, ‘ Gods of the Earth / Gods of the Sea’ (2005), sited on Kearfea hill, from where he Finlay’s Rousay (circa 1955). Courtesy Orkney Library and Archive. i n t r o d u c t i o n / 1 5 saw his dilapidated house looking out over the ‘timeless slab of grey or blue sea’ to Egilsay. 52 Finlay’s Orkney was distinctive—the islands still have a unique character—populated by a raft of quirky, genuine folk (represented in the poems as Big Jim, Mansie, Peedie Alice Mary, etc.) and writ ers (most importantly Ernest Marwick, George Mackay Brown and Robert Rendall)—characters whose folk charm suited the poet’s out look and poetic places with which he felt a kinship. 53 Like Dunira, the island is a precursor of ‘hyperborean’ Stonypath, which he liked to describe as an ‘Inland Garden’ as if to emphasize his longing for the sea, for Orkney or perhaps even the Bahamas of his birth. He gave each of the ponds that he dug in the garden a wee island, and each island a poem. For all its wildness, Rousay had a Platonic perfection, its con stituent parts—loch, mill and farms; the single road, upon which he worked as a labourer; the rugged coast—were, ‘being on an island . . . li ke a concrete poem, very particular, very realised.’ 54 Perthshire sto ries, Rousay lyrics, Stonypath garden poems: the formal evolution of Finlay’s work seems to settle into discrete locations; but these places are all ‘islanded’—could only be so, given the poet’s sensitive nature. Even the sea change discovery of Concrete poetry would only be a new means to represent the far firs of Dunira and tides of Rousay. 55 t h e d a n c e r s i n h e r i t t h e P a r t y When Finlay returned to Edinburgh in March 1959, he stayed in a number of rooms

and flats, the most famous of which was 24 Fettes Row at the foot of the Neoclassical New T own. 56 His emotional life was a shambles and the effects of his illness left him dependent on a succession of young women who acted as nurses and muses. Among these was Jessie McGuffie, whom he met in 1959 when she was still a 1 6 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n classics student, who would collaborate on Wild Hawthorn Press and their magazine, Poor. Old. Tired. Horse. 57 His letters describe how he feels ‘in a hell of tension and fears’; even walking in the streets is a terrifying experience, for it’s as if everyone ‘is other than they pretend, and there’s no stability. Anywhere.’ His symptoms are felt ‘as an inner force, that is detached from me and ought to be my aggression. Instead, it’s coming on me; I’ve got to learn to get it out.’ 58 He also complains of feelings of guilt in a kind of deep, radical way—laden with it. I feel this is a sign of living in touch with reality—(guilt in the moral sphere being equiv. to gravity in the physical)—but it also makes it imposs. to cope with reality. Madness and righteousness go together. It seems to me that the source of neurosis is the enormous social lie that everything is alright, when in fact it is a jungle just under the surface. Sin would matter little if it was faced instead of hidden. As it is, the social righteous people force others to bear their guilt. [ . . . ] But the whole force of society is on their side . . . Ho w can individual neurosis be helped in such a set up? It’s nonsense to try, I fe el. 59 The only comfort, he feels, is tenderness, ‘that people must gang up against the void’. 60 Finlay began to receive analysis for his illness, now diagnosed as agoraphobia, at the respected Davidson Clinic in Edin bu rgh, founded by the Jungian psychoanalyst Dr. Winifred Rushforth. 61 He also underwent treatment in a psychiatric ward of the Ross Clinic in Aberdeen: ‘How sordid hospital was. It sometimes seems to me that every social institution exists solely to conceal the absence of the quality it is meant to embody.’ 62 Back in Edinburgh

he ‘spent all summer having LSD25 (Mescaline) at the hospital, and ended up rather shattered’, for the treatment produced a succession of ‘horrid and frightening’ hallucinations of his early life, ‘evidently more perturbing than I realised . . . I feel as if some horrid truth is half out and the rest has to be faced.’ 63 Inevitably perhaps, the poet reacted against this i n t r o d u c t i o n / 1 7 regime, quarreling with his analyst. A letter to his publisher, Migrant Press, asks for the addition of a dedication to his poem ‘The Writer and Beauty’ for his analysts: ‘two people I detest, and I hope the poem slays them: poems are about the only weapons I have . . . O f course, it is a very pure poem, and not all bitter as they deserve’. 64 From this time we can date his rejection of psychology and the exposure of anguish, and his distaste for 1960s counter culture. Cure would come, if it came at all, through human fondness and art: ‘I must be about the only contem porary writer who believes that the purpose of art is to—oh dearie me, I forget exactly what—let’s say: be beautiful.’ 65 Finlay’s ideal of beauty remained pastoral and domestic—Rousay’s fish hook festooned cottage; Stonypath’s gliders, sailboats and donkeys. This fondness for childhood idylls, so familiar from the Perthshire sto ries, took on a new form at Fettes Row, where he borrowed a room from a friend and began to make wooden toys—‘boats, aeroplanes, a stove with a tall chimney and moon on top, a lollipop pot, a tower of umbrellas, fir tree with moon, a caravan, a billycan forest, a lopeared billycan, fish, etc.’—fond objects which offered him a way into the out side world even when trapped indoors. 66 This hobby was a stepping stone to his poem objects, which would in turn propose the creation of a garden—a kind green world in which he could immerse himself. In later years the nature of the toys changed; fishing boats metamorphos ing into destroyers. Through his deepening commitment to art the poet regained self belief. Philosophy guided him to the Stoics and he learned to redefine his agoraphobia as cultural homesickness, an antique yearn ing for the temples of the Greeks. Immersion in an Arcadian dreams cape also translated rage into

‘war’, as he became ever more determined to defend his art and safeguard the home it had shaped. The publication of his stories in The Sea Bed, in 1958, marked the end of Finlay’s attempts to capture a world in prose. Now came the struggle to realize his vision in poetry, with the appearance of his 1 8 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n first collection, The Dancers Inherit the Party (1960). The publication of The Dancers arose indirectly from a raft of new letter friendships with international poets, avant garde artists and publishers—Louis Zukofsky, Lorine Niedecker, Jerome Rothenberg, Ed Dorn, Robert Creeley, Jonathan Williams, Ronald Johnson, Robert Lax, Dick Higgins, Eugen Gomringer, Ernst Jandl, Dom Sylvester Houédard, Ad Reinhardt, Gustav Metzger and countless others. This was the era of the small press publishing revolution, which allowed Finlay to be in touch with new ideas and rapidly absorb new forms, and whose generous principles had a more lasting impact upon him than any par ticular variant of the avant garde. From this point on there was always a special bookshelf in Finlay’s house stacked with the work of innova tive poet publisher friends: Cid Corman (Origin), Thomas A. Clark and Laurie Clark (Moschatel), Stuart Mills (Tarasque), Simon Cutts (Coracle), and many others. Writing to Corman to thank him for the latest issue of Origin magazine, Finlay says how much encountering the work of Zukofsky and Niedecker means, for they confirm what I had felt (when I was writing on my own up in Orkney, never knowing all this stuff existed) should be done. Not the same, but the same world, or same relation to the world[. . . .] I just went by intuition; I fe lt—FELT —that what was being done here was all wrong and not traditional or modern either, because real tradition consists in feeling how poetry was, and out of that, how it should be now, etc.—not, that is, just parodying tradition. And what I wrote—there was no one to say, that is right or wrong; I wished awfully I could go and ask God, Does this come off? For otherwise one stays awake all night worrying [. . .] Well, what I like best to try and do is to write something that stands on a wire, and then leans very far over, as far as it can

go—Does it fall, or not? 67 In the summer of 1960, Finlay initiated a correspondence with Michael Shayer, assistant to the Scottish poet Gael T urnbull, a doctor living in Ventura, California, from where he published Migrant maga i n t r o d u c t i o n / 1 9 zine. He sent Shayer a sheaf of recent poems, some of which appeared in issues 7 and 8. The editors quickly agreed to Finlay’s suggestion of a book, which was published in October 1960. The poems crafted scenes of beauty dearly needed, and its publication marked a shift in the Scottish poetry scene. The Edinburgh Finlay had returned to was sparking to life in a series of jerks, as Scottish culture was shucked free from mediocrity and dourness. There were bouts of ‘flyting’ in the press (1959–1960) between folk song revivalists and the old guard of ‘makars’, for whom MacDiarmid still held sway. The Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962) was an epochal flashpoint, spurring anti nuclear marches against the American naval bases on the River Clyde. Even the International Writers Festival (20–24 August 1962) had a stramash, when the stern Stalinist MacDiarmid clashed with his nemesis, ‘cosmopolitan scum’ Alexander Trocchi. 68 A new scene was taking shape around the American Jim Haynes’s Paperback Bookshop and coffee houses such as Studio Three, run by Finlay’s friends Lesley Lendrum and Janet Sideman. The bustle of the Festival ‘packed with poets’ exhausted Finlay, and he wrote Mackay Brown of nightly readings where ‘my Orkney poems . . . h ave been the smash hit.’ 69 His poems were read by Paul Pond (later Paul Jones of Manfred Mann’s Earth Band); also per forming were Anselm Hollo, Michael Horovitz, Pete Brown and The Mersey Beat poets, Adrian Henri, Roger McGough and Brian Patten: ‘all with anti Bomb badges, all very gentle and sweet’. 70 He schooled them how to say ‘peedie’ and ‘cuithes’ in Orcadian, but, ‘they aren’t MY SET and I don’t have a set now, and they are very much a set so you feel outside of it—but it was nice. There just weren’t any ones like that when I was wee. Otherwise, the older people here, the emerged ones— I have this def. feeling that it is all a waste of time, they have a different kind of sensibility—it’s not ideas, it’s something more basic, I just feel

lost with them, they seem like part of something that is OVER.’ 71 2 0 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n The time had come to make new alliances, however rackety. T ogether with his friend the poet and folk singer Hamish Henderson, and the Glaswegian poet Edwin Morgan, Finlay helped shape a Scottish avant garde that was oddly homely, less a programmatic move ment than a fey shoulder pressed against the wheel of the moribund Scottish Renaissance. 72 Morgan summed up their ethos in an essay, ‘The Beatnik in the Kailyard’: ‘The Renaissance has begun to loosen its hold on life’, MacDiarmid has banished ‘ordinary human sympa thy’. 73 Henderson in turn accused MacDiarmid of a ‘kind of spiritual apartheid’. Finlay wrote Jerome Rothenberg, ‘There is a feeling in the air just now of relaxation, with therefore more signs of communication between people. Most obviously happening in Russia.’ 74 T o encour age this thawing the three poets interwove strands of folk culture, contemporary poetry, art and a hotchpotch of sentiment—Morgan’s fallen ‘cuddy’ cart horse (drawn from Mayakofsky) and Finlay’s sad coal horse, sweet little Beat windmill turning in the west, and tender friends walking through seaweed. Finlay drew his inspiration from new American poet friends, correspondents, and visits from Robert Creeley, Jerome and Diane Rothenberg, Jonathan Williams and Ronald Johnson. 75 Morgan added his translations of comrade poets from the Eastern Bloc in his playful ‘Sovpoem’ versions of Pasternak, Voznesensky, Y evtushenko and Attila József. 76 His and Morgan’s adventure found its culmination in what was then the epitome of innovation, Concrete poetry. Wild Hawthorn and Poor. Old. Tired. Horse. — POTH, as it became fondly known—were the crucial outlets for all these innovations, and, determined to keep the new movement open, Finlay sketched his aims in broad terms: ‘panache, humour, beauty, tradition and experiment.’ 77 He had no interest in experiment for its own sake and, although POTH came to represent the new movement, unlike other Scottish magazines of the period, there was no ‘party line’; the maga i n t r o d u c t i o n / 2 1 zine extolled his timeless themes, the sea and domestic life. 78 Wild Hawthorn had a similarly international platform. Planned selections of Karl Kraus, Attila József, and Cuban poets (with an introduction by Fidel Castro), failed to appear

due to lack of funds, but illustrated collections by Lorine Niedecker, Louis Zukofsky, Gael T urnbull and Erik Satie (translated by Ronald Johnson and illustrated by John Furnival) are now much sought after. Each publication was a blue print, as Finlay worked his way through modern design styles: neue typographie for Concrete poems; Art Nouveau for Satie, Apollinaire and Max Jacob. 79 The Russian Futurists, Schwitters, Arp and Hugo Ball appeared alongside neglected figures such as the Scottish poet Hamish Maclaren. He also worked with gifted designers and typog raphers such as Edward Wright, and benefited from the patient help of his printer friend, Michael Hamish Glen. Finlay’s practice as a publisher anticipated his early gardens, as a kind of laboratory, and, like those gardens, it was always a collabora tive enterprise. In the most successful collaborations he discerned his vision of a totalized artwork, intuiting the combination of effects that would soon be realized in the ‘garden poem’. 80 Finlay enthused about other technologies; he wanted Wild Hawthorn to produce records— one of football supporters’ songs and commentaries, another of his poems and songs by the folk singer Robin Hall, or performed by the popular actor Stanley Baxter. 81 He always loved football; a letter to Robert Creeley reports Scotland beating England in their annual match: ‘it was splendid [. . .] They played beautifully, like I am always saying [the poets] should start and write: precisely, laconically . . . oh , it was wonderful; the first time Scotland has won for about two decades—I really felt it was a big victory for The Wild Hawthorn approach.’ 82 This fondness for popular art forms and new technology was hardly a matter of fashion, although Finlay does write sweetly to Edwin Morgan offering to play him ‘a lovely Elvis Presley record’ if he will come over from Glasgow for a visit. 83 References to pop music

and foot ball were one cause of the arguments with MacDiarmid and his allies, who were soon patronizing Finlay and his ‘beatnik’ pals as uppity insurgents and ‘TEDDYBOY POETASTERS’. 84 Hostile reviews began to appear, such as Maurice Lindsay’s attack in New Saltire, ‘quite gratuitous, accusing us of printing “Poor. Y oung. Trite. Verse”, and of being for the new and fashionable at any price.’ 85 The same issue car ried a review of The Dancers —‘typically eccentric doodles’, and of Wild i n t r o d u c t i o n / 2 3 Hawthorn’s Lorine Niedecker booklet, ‘scruffy little pamphlet . . . “neo surrealistic scrawls”. ’ Worse was to follow, when Hugh MacDiarmid published a pamphlet, The Ugly Bird Without Wings, attacking Finlay as ‘degenerate’. Feeling that there was ‘no alternative but to fight’, he wrote Niedecker, ‘I who was once rather gentle and tolerant, am now going to make them RUE THE DAY THEY showed their contempt for beauty . . . I ’m going to fight them to the death—the whole horrible lot.’ 86 In a printed sheet inserted inside the third number of POTH, Finlay railed: ‘We began with a feeling of warmth and open ness. We are now going to return hate for hate.’ 87 He also conceived the first of his battle scenarios, a happening inspired protest march, gleefully described to Creeley: there was no march of course as no one here is on our side, but we invented it, and I said there would be a zeppelin, taschiste banners, enormous balloons, etc., and that we would march on The Writers’ Conference; so everyone believed it, and the magistrates made a special Order to ban it, ‘March Banned BUT Feud Goes On’ as one paper headlined it; then they reported on the radio that we planned to burn effigies of public figures in the streets . . . n ervous trouble or not, we took a taxi up [to The Scotsman newspaper] and Jessie [McGuffie] punched the literary editor. 88 T o Corman he noted the bravado of the enterprise, ‘the Myth was greater than the March could ever have been . . . Well, I always did say that myth could be a powerful weapon.’ 89 And to Rothenberg he enthused about the ‘didactic creative’ excitement: ‘I begin to feel why people like to have revolutions—to sense the patterns,

and bet on them, and see them emerge—sheer delight!’ 90 T wo decades later Finlay refined this ‘delight’ into a specific revolution, that of Robespierre and Saint Just, actualizing the ‘zeppelin myth’, in the form of a replica Panzer tank defending his garden. 91 2 4 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n t r u l y t r a d i t i o n a l . a n d n e w , o f n o w Like all Scottish poets of his generation, Finlay had to work out an aes thetic response to the craggy edifice of MacDiarmid and the question of language and Nationalism. The ‘Orkney Lyrics’ are playful homage to MacDiarmid’s early lyrics while at the same time teasing the didacti cism of the late epic poems . With hindsight, there are striking paral lels between the two poets: contrarian in a typically Scottish manner, they share radical and reactionary tendencies. Both defined the poet’s role in terms of absolutes, and their political idealism became infused with antinomian violence. T o escape Scottish parochialism they bus ied themselves with internationalist peers. Creatively, they both found innovative ways to outreach conventions of authorship, playing with quotation, found text, and the epic, in the very different forms of the MacDiarmidian heroic long poem and Finlayian poetry garden. Finlay characterized MacDiarmid’s reanimation of Scots as a weird compound, as a dead language ‘animated by some freak electric energy.’ 92 In a parodic homage he composed his pioneering Glaswegian menagerie, Glasgow Beasts (1961), reinventing the Scots idiom by meld ing together the vernacular of music hall and folk song with the zen poems of Japanese poet Shimpei Kusano. In doing so he became the first British poet to bring together innovative poetic form and the potential of contemporary dialect. Other early poems from The Dancers bear out this fascination with folk idioms and, writing to Hamish Henderson, he outlined his attempts to do folk over again with ‘ironic sophistica tion’, offering ‘ Angles of Stamps’ as an example: ‘I’m sick of folk as a DEAD thing . . . W e are surely very narrow if we understand only one culture (they talk of two cultures, but it seems to me there are twenty two. And all of value).’ 93 Finlay offered artistic precedents for his use of ‘Glasgow Scots’,

such as the Russian Futurists, who ‘used street— folk —speech (such as I horrified local folk by doing in Glasgow Beasts ), Le Circus (or, Poster Poem) (1964). Finlay’s first poem-print, and the first poem to be defined in this way in modern English poetry. He explains: ‘the form of the poem suggests a poster for the circus. The fishing-boat K47 is compared to a pony, its port and starboard lights to coloured blinkers, the crew to bare-back riders, the rainbow and its reflection on the sea to a hoop. The corks, nets, “etc.” are introduced like lesser parts of the act.’ (Letter to Emmett Williams, 7 January 1967, RSCL.) The original is printed in black, red, and blue. Finlay’s poem-prints adopt the ‘poeme-pancarte’ pioneered by the French poet Pierre Albert-Birot in the 1920s. Finlay wrote Stephen Bann of his plan: ‘I’d like to start a series of single-sheet largeish poem-prints—you know, to frame like a print of a painting, only they’d be concrete poems’ (28 October 1964). In 1964 Wild Hawthorn Press published ‘Le Circus’ as part of just such a series of ‘poem-prints’: ‘EPITAPH FÜR KONRAD BAYER’, Franz Mon; ‘PARADIS’, Pierre Albert-Birot; ‘ PO EM / PR INT ’, F erdinand Kriwet; ‘P OL AR ’, J ohn Furnival. 2 6 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n and the painters, too, were crazy about folk art, and USED it in their work.’ 94 Being born far from Scotland he had no direct access to ‘the local idiom’ and the ease of self expression it could bring, nor did he feel able to settle for the preeminent literary Nationalism of the day. 95 T o Rothenberg he speculated whether his father’s financial downfall had caused him to lose his own ‘class syntax’. 96 In poems such as ‘T wice’, ‘Scene’ and ‘Dalchonzie’, we catch the poet in the midst of these investigations, much as he sees his friend Robert Creeley doing: Your poetry is very Scottish, not that it’s like how S. poets write, but like how they ought to write if they made a proper use of their moral past. In fact, the movement of your poems is very Glasgow . . . a nd the Glasgow movement is (probably) the result of the mixture of Scottish & Irish . . . I a m talking about two different things, the

way your poetry is moral, and the way it moves, like its tempo, but something more inner than tempo. Well, that is one of the great pleasures of it. As for moral, I mean like T olstoy is moral, not when he is moralising, but when he does that amaz ing thing of presenting a moral statement as a physical sensation. 97 These concerns anticipate Concrete poetry. It is clear why the new poetics was so welcome, providing him with the means to revolution ize syntax and structure—the ‘being’ of a poem—beyond anything that was being attempted in Scotland or cosmopolitan London. The foreignness of it all chimed with his own feelings, for it belonged to the worldwide political and social thaw. New models of poetic con struction arrived via a constant flurry of aerograms from poets with exotic addresses—Sao Paulo, Kyoto, Vienna. This kinship was deeply felt because it was still almost impossible for Finlay to leave his room and, being ‘cut off from the world’ he felt disconnected from the ‘ordi nary syntax’ of ‘social reality’. 98 The Concrete poem offered a model of order, ‘even if set in a space which is full of doubt’. 99 Finlay spoke of his faith in Concrete as something ‘honest’ and ‘true’, not in terms of Star / Steer (1968). than potatoes’; poems ‘like little snowflakes, just about to melt’—and Finlay feels himself to be utterly at the ‘end of poems that are about’ —now all he wants to do are ‘poems that just are.’ 104 3 0 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n Although still frequently referred to by the epithet ‘Concrete poet’, from the beginning Finlay understood the movement had many aspects and possibilities. In A Little Anthology of Concrete Poetry, a primer he edited for Rothenberg’s Great Bear pamphlet series (unpublished), he included poems by the painter poets Klee and Kandinsky, to remind the reader ‘the movement has no “absolute” birth.’ 105 Concrete was defined by the work of poet friends, in particular the Swiss, Eugen Gomringer, and the de Campos brothers of Brazil, whose work he preferred for their variations on classical calm, and the abstract poems of the American Robert Lax. Stuck in the city, the landscapes of Rousay and Perthshire remained utmost in the poet’s mind. He admitted to having little feeling for ‘space ages . . . I still love the old themes—I often think all my subsequent work is just my stories done over again, in different ways.’ 107 What was new was a poetics of representation, defining, even belonging to a place, for he could already see that ‘so many of these poems would be nice if done in glass—I mean, on glass—and set out in a garden . . . o r in a landscape.’ 108 The scenes themselves seemed to invite him to take that radical step back into the world—fraught as the prospect was—and, if the poem now required a landscape,

then the poet himself would require a home. This new surge of creativity was shadowed by the struggle to find ‘an unambiguous situation’ emotionally and morally, for Finlay contin ued to feel harried by poverty and illness: ‘the feeling of alienation can get so ingrained, and one must act in spite of it, and try to keep calm . . . So metimes I feel that even a modest peace is difficult to achieve. Other times I feel able to go on trying.’ 109 As always, the possibility of achiev ing such peace lay with the loving support of a woman, or women. In 1964, Jessie McGuffie left for America to marry Dick Sheeler (an ex student of Louis Zukofsky). All the while he endured uncertain health and constant poverty. Creatively the new forms resolved themselves as a ‘poemorama’: the means to model pine woods and islands or represent voyages imaginatively. 112 In a burst of activity he created an incredible diversity of touching scenes from the world he was painfully sequestered from—innovative kinetic poems and sequential bookworks; colourful ‘poster poems’ with diverse typographies; unfolding journeys he could not make himself through the rhythm of pages turned; the canal with its jolly barge sailing slowly by; the port bustling with lemon shaped fishing boats; and the little fish leaping in a longed for burn. Finally, with the support of friends and lovers and culminating with the arrival of Sue’s pivotal influence, this anticipatory delight returned him once more to the reality of a Highland home. Gledfield Farmhouse, on the Dornoch Firth, was the first of his garden retreats; there he wove a little community around himself according to his needs. Now Finlay could real ize his youthful dream of an ideal place, where the word might be at home in the world and the world be only that home, by the new means of translating poem objects into a permanent setting, with the addition 3 6 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n of flowers, woodland groves and, eventually, grottoes and temples. For, as he wrote Mary Ellen Solt: ‘the new means of constructing a poem aesthetically, ought to lead to consideration of new materials. If these poems are for “contemplating”, let them be made with that intention, and let them be sited where they can be contemplated.’ 119 The garden poem combined the spatial and temporal possibilities of his poem prints and bookworks with Sue’s intuitive feeling for planting. His break throughs always preceded theorizing; he intuited the potential of the outdoor poem long before he became acquainted with the literature of the landscape tradition. As crucial as the ambience of antiquity would become, Finlay proceeded as a poet, one who is guided by language. The beginnings of that process are vivid in his letters to Stephen Bann reporting a busy time at Gledfield, cutting letters for an outdoor version of ‘little fields / long horizons’ (1965)—a poem which perfectly encapsulates his relationship to place, that longing for the bounded, the terror of distance and romance of new horizons: ‘It is really fascinating to work large, and astonishing how one’s sense of scale changes [ . . . ] “L ittle fields”—if I ever got the wood and wall to finish it—would be 35 feet long [ . . . ] It soon feels natural, and only when people pass the house do you remember that such activities must be considered eccentric.’ 120 The shift from Modernism toward cottage and classical idioms begins with him ‘pondering a possible relationship between certain concrete poems and the kind of inscriptions that are carved on tombstones [ . . . ] O ne could argue that the inscriptions are brief, and often set small in a large space, because each letter must be carved; but it would be equally true to note that the brevity is part—as the space is part—of some

kind of implicit statement about life, death, and time.’ 121 In November 1967, at Stonypath, his first ‘wee poem carved by the local tombstone maker’ arrived; already he can envisage it ‘outside, among lots of wee ponds and things.’ 122 i n t r o d u c t i o n / 3 7 Now began the exhausting process of experimenting with new materials and design styles for, as Finlay tells Creeley, it’s high time Concrete poetry ‘came of age and had the same standards of produc tion as any other art that has a visual element.’ 123 Finlay writes the artist Henry Clyne, an important early collaborator, about the visionary ideas which ‘haunt me’, formal, dignified structures, in which the poem is not eccentric or bizarre, but as natural as the inscription on a stone of a memorial [ . . . ] concrete poetry offers [ . . . ] a way of bringing that art right back into the very centre of society—i.e. into architecture [ . . . ] the pure concrete poem is i nexhaustible; it is not for reading but for contemplating [ . . . ] All this is q uite new, and I think no one—not even the poets—has quite understood the possibilities. Far from concrete poetry being an end [ . . . ] it i s really only a beginning [ . . . ] I think the garden, and the church, and the side of the block of flats, are the places for poems—only, of course, such poems ought to be dignified, and formal, and austere. 124 The progress of his thinking had a vitalizing effect on POTH, cul minating in the sympathetic integration of text and image in a succes sion of collaborative issues: Robert Lax and Emil Antonucci (No. 17 , December 1965), Ronald Johnson and John Furnival (No. 19, Sep te mber 1966), Ad Reinhardt and Bridget Riley (No. 18, c. Being somehow connected, they form a corner in language . .

I would be so pleased if you could send at least a dozen—or more, if you can . . . Y ear by year the composed landscape distinguished itself from the wild hillside and the broad waste of the moor. Finlay extolled the ‘slow excitement’ of his new art. 153 His imaginative fancy conjured Stonypath as a belated epi sode in the English landscape garden tradition—those ‘quite extraor dinary PURE SYMPHONIC creations’, in which nature is poeticized, abstracted: pond as Pool, grass as Lawn, sundial gnomon dividing shadow into measure and order. 154 When the first turf was turned over at Stonypath his involvement in the international avant garde began to wane: turning towards his own vale he rediscovered the didactic and, in time, the epic. History began to age Stonypath. The toys of childhood were supplanted by sober Hellene columns; the charming pensée refined into the mossy wit of the detached sentence. Culture offered solace and comfort, redeemed wild nature—even the ‘untutored’ pebble of the seashore was required to bear a poem. Homesick beyond the bounds of the self, the poet had enacted a radical withdrawal, which in turn set in motion a wave of self translation—not a chronological wave sweeping on nostalgia back to the shores of ancient Rome and Greece; but a race of currents— ph ilosophy, i n t r o d u c t i o n / 4 7 the masque of history, war, revolution—all caught up in the surging undertow of poetics and myth. Over the course of the next two decades, Finlay tested the lyrical, the pure, the heroic and the tragic, one against the other, seeking a conception of wholeness that was both new and ancient. Any lingering worries that the work might appear ‘eccentric’ to the casual bystander were banished. The reward for his labours on the garden was a stance: to enter the gate was to accept his determined vision of this world. This ‘model of order’ was not, however, a hermeti cally sealed enclosure; rather, his new work was interrogative, accusa tory of the age, determined to acknowledge fury, power and destruc tion. Returning to the Stonypath of 1971, we catch Finlay announcing the latest of his summer revolutions to Bann, tongue in cheek: Did I tell you I have (meanwhile) fallen in love with battleships? This body of work unleashed a storm, and the final years of the decade descended into an almost mythical scenario—one beyond his and Sue’s control—in which his fury was matched by the hostility of critics, jeal ous conspirators and the internecine struggles of Mitterand’s Paris. The very vituperativeness of these disputes, on all sides, was a final proof of the inability of rational thought to absorb these difficult truths, or of culture to civilize them. Finlay’s didactic vision of the Revolution is a radical projection of characteristics we cannot help but recognize in the poet himself: the shadowed bedchamber of Robespierre, who has been taken from his home to the scaffold; the red thread of mourning tied

around the vic tim’s neck, emblematic of loss. By a heroic act of the disaffected will, the poet exile has transferred his own feelings of homelessness back onto the world, saying, pace Joseph Beuys: ‘everything is wrong’, ‘every thing must change’. 176 Is the bloodstained blade and its torrent of heads really to be the guarantor of our piety? T o his longstanding collaborator Gary Hincks, Finlay offered some reassurance: ‘T error is the piety of the Revolution’ is one of the most difficult texts in the Garden T emple—deliberately so [. . .] Obviously, the ‘terror’ theme stands along with the military themes as being against the assumptions of the present age. Equally obviously, it does not stand alone, but relates to other themes such as The Sublime, which was the great discovery of the 18th century; in one sense one could place the guillotine beside the Alps in a pantheon of T error. My point is this: not all that glitters is gold and not all that appears liberal is spiritual or proceeds from moral convic tion, or conviction of any kind [. . .] The universe of the modern liberal is a fiction (because it excludes all the elements of ‘the given’ which he does not like to think about); but the point is that it is also an impoverished fiction because it excludes the tragic, the sublime, and (in the end) the serious; it is not even ‘nice’ (since even nice ness, as we know, is suspect 5 8 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n to modern cynicism). Anyway, the T error saying is so difficult that it has to be grasped by intuition rather than explicated; but set in the perspec tive of Poussin and Diderot, it loses some of its unacceptability (I hope). 177 The thunderous air that hangs around the brooding figure of Saint Just inspired a series of Revolutionary fragments and declamations; texts which, even graven in stone, burn with feeling. Balancing the insurrectionary mood are the poet’s somber meditations, as the era of rebellion gradually gives way to an era of contemplation, and the gar den itself matures to enclose the still shadows of a cypress grove. The work gathered to itself a Biblical cast: Saint Just assumes the guise of a Christ like martyr, Robespierre that of an Old T estament prophet. This

O f course Robespierre’s Speeches are really Sermons and the whole discourse of the Revolution is in a sense theology.’ 179 Despite this atmosphere of steeples, clerestories and altars, despite having his own T emple, Finlay was no eccentric cultist. His cause had adherents, but the Garden T emple held no chthonian rites. The Saint Just Vigilantes formalized his need to be protected by friends— ‘Friends are placed beside each other in battle’—and we can discern that same need for tenderness in his sentences on Friendship: ‘Friends who seem to have deserted / us may have deserted themselves.’ 180 This decade of conflict had a severe cost, contributing to his separation from Sue, and without her protective support he gradually withdrew from such severe forms of flyting. 181 t h e w i l d f l o w e r We are familiar with the way Finlay’s creativity shaped itself around collaborative relationship and, in the 1990s, this role was fulfilled by the Hungarian curator Pia Maria Simig. If Sue was most at home in the garden, Pia’s expertise was in the gallery and artworld; her skill

in co creating installations, and her ability to promote the poet’s work through a series of major international exhibitions did much to cement his reputation as an artist. As well as completing large scale permanent projects in Britain and Europe, together they created his second com plete garden, Fleur De l’ Air, in Provence (1997–2003). For the first time in his life, Finlay was financially secure. He took the opportunity to expand the garden into new areas of Stonypath; the old paddock where the family donkeys, Serpolette, Artemis and Maus 6 0 \ i n t r o d u c t i o n grazed, became the English Parkland, with a teasing ‘Huff Lane’ for Pia. He also laid down plans for the last area, a Medieval Hortus Conclusus, secured within the walls of the old hay barn, completed after his death. The garden had always been an act of imagination, even clairvoy ance; the projection of impersonations of other vistas and landscapes within his own five acres, worlds within worlds. Now Robespierre gradually faded to Rousseau. The poet returned to model making and summer was once again lit up with glider idylls. He also took up gar dening as a hobby, walked the moorland bounds and enjoyed wander ing the woodland paths of the garden he and Sue had created. There unfolded a last long autumnal decade whose emblems were the wild flower and fishing boat, and whose ideal literary form was the proverb. Sometimes Finlay expressed puzzlement that he had lost the energy for battles. In truth his imagination had returned to the pastoral, in poems which recalled the early days at Stonypath, celebrating the moor, with its larks and bog cotton, and the wild roses that grew by the burn. There was also a return to forms that had inspired him years ago, such as the haiku, in Flakes (1990) and Spring Verses (1993), and the Concrete poem, in such works as ‘Lines of Foam’ (1997). There was still some yearning for the past, emblematized in homages to Novalis and Goethe, but the voyages he made through Time were as likely to circle around his own past: for instance, offering Novalis’s ‘blue flower’ as a commemoration of his own ‘blue sail’; or Goethe’s beloved lemon trees for his own fishing boats, themselves now passing into memory. In the earlier years at Stonypath, Finlay fondly referred to

his home as an ‘ Autumn thought’. Now, in his final years, he rediscovered the garden and its moor as the only idyll to which he could ever truly return. The relationship between the actual and the ideal righted itself; the border demarking cultivation and wild nature blurred. A form of truce declared itself, in his feelings; the garden gate was no longer an i n t r o d u c t i o n / 6 1 armed frontier. The garden too found acceptance as a much loved work of art which Scotland had taken to its heart. Most extraordinary of all, the defining condition of his exile altered as, following a stroke, he rediscovered a freedom to travel and began to revisit the haunts of his youth. Ian Hamilton Finlay died on 27 March 2006. He was buried in a fam ily grave near Hopetoun House. On the gravestone, after his name, there appears only the one word: ‘Poet’. Flowers in a garden are an acceptable eccentricity. Poussin and Salvator: Cops and Robbers. Modern sculpture is willfully ignorant. Superior gardens are composed of Glooms and Solitudes and not of plants and trees. A liberal’s compost heap is his castle. Solitude in gardens is an aspect of scale . Camouflage is the last form of classical landscape painting. It represents not this tree or that field but Fields and Trees. Gardens are always for next year. British Weather is often warmer at weeding level. ‘Only connect’ — E. M . Forster. (And affect — I. H . F .) Garden centres must become the Jacobin Clubs of the new Revolution. Grand conceptions are inhuman to small inhuman minds. Gardens were first categorised in terms of Emperors, then of architects, and nowadays of mere sculptors — a barbarous decline. Our earth is carnivorous. Embark on a garden with a Vision but never with a plan. Public funding of the arts should be confined to nations with heroic ideologies. The lawn is the garden’s downfall. Gardening activity is of five kinds, namely, sowing, planting, fixing, placing, maintaining. In so far as gardening is an Art, all these may be taken under the one head, composing. l a t e r w r i t i n g s / 1 8 1 Take a small grove of pine trees

and dry pave the ground with common brick. Now sweep the fallen pine needles around the base of each tree. Where the viewer is solitary, imagination is the scale. Better than truth to materials is truth to intelligence. In our climate, why should we not provide some of our garden features at least with shadow — formed, say, of brick — in lieu of the sun? Et in Arcadia ego : the cool root of stone, pleasing to the earthworm, renders the classical (as opposed to the plant) garden very vulnerable to the mole. Strawberries grown in hollow logs stood upright, are not inferior to small orchards, in the pleasure given by the bark, and leaves, and fruit. Formal gardens are (as it were) statues of Nature. A little too much is just enough for July. It is permissible, in the Art of gardening, to substitute a mooring post for a boat. What an extraordinary apparition is a tree in leaf! The inscription seems out of place in the modern garden. It jars on our secularism by suggesting the hierarchies of the word . The sundial’s true content is Time, the clock’s is the time. The pagan sundial tells the hour by a beam, the Christian by a shadow. Common brick will not form a lasting garden path. But it is instantly friendly to people, and plants and trees. Sundials only appear to tell the time; rather, they tell old cottages, silence, cumulus clouds, elm trees, steeples, and moss. J Rousseau. Modern refinement has made THE PEBBLE almost a relative of the Fairies. PEBBLES are most prized by those whose temperament discovers a dangerous possibility of controversy in simple apples and pears. A PEBBLE is a form of perfect vacuity, as a wild flower is of modesty. Children pile up PEBBLES as pin less hand grenades. The modern PEBBLE is prized as a sculpture, as it were, of a PEBBLE. Kettle’s Yard, in Cambridge, England, is the Louvre of the PEBBLE. T o inscribe words on PEBBLES would be a desecration if thought knew no hierarchies. Making PEBBLES skip is an obvious resort of misanthropy. (This with apologies to Hazlitt.) The Victory of David proved the advantage, not of the smaller size of the missile, but of the superior range. The boulder of Goliath would have been the right retort to the PEBBLE of David. Beside a true work of sculpture, the PEBBLE has the advantage (to the modern mind), that it is no sort of T est. The wide appreciation of PEBBLES is a remote consequence of Protestantism. The PEBBLE never had so much dignity as when it was employed as an alpha by the old Pythagoreans. The PEBBLE is foolishly admired as being hand made by the Ocean.
